title: Pingala the Courtesan's Renunciation
story:
A wandering teacher, one of those who take their lessons from the world itself, used to say that among his teachers was a woman he had never met — a courtesan named Pingala, in the city of Videha. He spoke of her with the respect a student owes a teacher, for the lesson she had taught him had cost her a long and sleepless night.

Pingala lived by waiting. Each evening she dressed herself and adorned herself and went to the door of her house to wait for a man — a client, one who would come with money, for money was what she lived by. One night a man had promised to come to her, and so she stood at the door and watched the road. The evening fell, the lamps were lit along the street, and still he did not come. He had said he would come, but the street had emptied, and the road she watched stayed bare.

She waited, watching every man who passed. At each approaching footstep her hope rose; at each stranger who walked on by, it fell. The night wore on. The lamps burned low, and the door grew cold against her shoulder. Her face grew thin and drawn, her thoughts small and weary, and still she leaned in the doorway, holding herself together with nothing but the hope of a man who never came.

Then, in the dead of the night, something in her turned. It was not despair exactly — or if it was, it was the despair that sets a person free. She looked at herself leaning in that doorway, a woman dressed and waiting for a man who would not come, and she saw, with a sudden and terrible clarity, what she had been doing with her life, and for how many nights, and for how little.

“Look at the depth of my delusion,” she said to herself. “I have worn myself out for a man who brings a little money, when the giver of all joy, the one who grants every gift, is near me always, and I never once turned to him. What I have chased so wretchedly, let me give it up.” She saw, then, how needlessly she had tormented herself, night after night, for so small and passing a thing.

She looked down at the body she had dressed so carefully, and she saw it for what it was — a thing of bone and skin and hair, a house with nine doors, one for each opening of the body, that leaks and fills with what is foul. So much trouble, she thought, for a thing that would not last. And she wondered what she had been offering, and to whom, and why it had ever seemed worth a single sleepless night.

Then she cut off her hope — not the quiet hope of ordinary days, but the grasping, hungry hope that had kept her leaning at the door. She turned from the road and sat down, and the street that had held her eyes all night went dark and quiet behind her. For the first time in longer than she could remember, she slept, and she slept in peace, the way a person sleeps when she owes no one anything.

The wandering teacher remembered her for this. A woman who had spent her nights waiting for what would not come, he said, had done in a single hour what scholars struggle a whole lifetime to do. And he kept her words as his own: hope is the greatest of pains, and freedom from hope the greatest of joys.
reflection: The story is careful not to make Pingala's peace a lesson for the poor or the lonely. What she gives up is not her life but her grasping — the hope that kept her leaning at a door for a man who never came, while the giver of every joy was, she realized, already near. Her “despair” is not a collapse but a release.
hero_scene: Pingala leaning in her doorway in the lamplit night, watching the empty road, her face worn thin with waiting.

a mood of longing giving way to peace
